claims.text: `git commit --all --message '<text>'` commits every tracked file that has changed, in one step, without a separate `git add`.
`git log --oneline` prints one line per commit: the abbreviated commit id followed by the first line of the commit message.

Each block of changed lines, together with the few unchanged lines Git prints around it (three by default), is a hunk, marked by a line starting `@@`; changes close enough to share those surrounding lines fall into one hunk. The hunk is the unit `git add --patch` offers you one at a time.
`git revert <commit>` records a new commit that reverses the changes introduced by the named commit; it does not remove that commit from the history.
`git bisect` performs a binary search over a range of commits, checking out a midpoint each round, to find the first commit where a symptom appears.
`git add --patch <file>` presents the file's changed hunks one at a time and asks whether to stage each; answering `y` stages that hunk, `n` leaves it in the working directory only.
claims.source_hint: git-add(1), --patch and INTERACTIVE MODE / patch mode prompt

claims.text: `git blame <file>` annotates each line of the file with the commit that last modified that line.
Git's own documentation recommends a commit message shaped as a summary line of no more than 50 characters, then a blank line, then a fuller description.
claims.source_hint: git-commit(1), DISCUSSION (first paragraph on message shape)

claims.text: Git checks neither the 50-character subject length nor the blank second line when you commit: that shape is a convention, not a rule Git applies to the message you write.
claims.source_hint: git-commit(1), DISCUSSION ("Though not required…"); no length or shape check documented in OPTIONS

claims.text: The example repository's file `docs/git/commit-message-examples.md` at tag `stage-0` states four rules: first line ≤ 50 characters in the imperative, blank second line, body saying why and which option was rejected, one commit = one separately revertable change.

The same file's bad example is five short messages that nobody, the author included, can interpret three months later; its good example's body says why cancelling a paid order is blocked (refunds not built) and rejects marking it "awaiting refund" because nobody watches that state.
Conventional Commits is a convention that requires a fixed prefix on the subject line; the Đơn Hàng rule file docs/git/commit-message-examples.md at `stage-0` does not ask for one.
`git switch --quiet -c <name> <start-point>` creates a branch at the start point and makes it the current branch.

`git diff --stat` summarises changes per file plus a total line of files changed, insertions and deletions; in the captured output it reports `1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)` for `README.md`.
`git add --patch` reads its answers from standard input, so `printf 'y\nn\n' |` supplies them without a person typing.

`git diff --cached` shows what is staged for the next commit, while `git diff` with no options shows changes in the working directory that are not staged; `working tree`, the script's word for that directory, is Git's own name for it.
claims.source_hint: git-diff(1), git diff --cached and git diff forms; gitglossary(7), entry "working tree"

claims.text: In the captured output of `scripts/git/stage-partial.sh`, staged and unstaged diffs hold one `@@` line each. Text after the second `@@` is an earlier file line Git repeats as a hunk label, not part of the hunk.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/stage-partial.txt lines 26-51; git-diff(1) / gitattributes(5), hunk header ("Defining a custom hunk-header")

claims.text: A commit should hold one logical change — the unit that can be reverted on its own — rather than whatever a work session touched.
When a subject line needs the word "and" to describe the change, the work is two commits.
Commit messages are worth writing when the reasoning is still fresh, because reconstructing why from an old diff means inventing it.

The commit message is the only reasoning Git stores inside the commit itself, so it is the only one that travels with the change wherever the commit goes; the code records the current state only. (`git notes` attaches later prose, but in a separate ref.)
claims.source_hint: git-commit(1), DESCRIPTION (the log message recorded with the commit); gitglossary(7), commit object; git-notes(1), DESCRIPTION
